why_this_tool: AWS publishes the Well-Architected Framework and a set of decision guides whose criteria and comparison tables give you real material for scoping, recording decisions and reviewing a design, all from a laptop and without running paid resources.
alternatives: Azure Well-Architected Framework and Google Cloud Architecture Framework offer similar pillar-based review guidance for their own clouds; adr-tools scaffolds decision records from the command line but gives no selection criteria; Structurizr, Mermaid and PlantUML render C4 diagrams as code but do not help choose what goes in the boxes; Google Docs or Markdown on GitHub hold the design doc itself and its review history.

setup.do: Sign in to the AWS Management Console with a free tier account; nothing in this path needs a paid resource, and if you have no account you can work from the documentation alone.
setup.done_when: You see the console home page after signing in, or you have noted that you will follow the path from the documentation only.

source.title: What is the AWS Management Console? - AWS Management Console

setup.why: The console is where you would later look up services and run a formal review, so you should know how to reach it. No step here creates billable resources.

setup.do: Read how AWS security credentials work and confirm you are signed in as a non-root identity.
setup.done_when: You can name the credential type you signed in with and it is not the root user.

source.title: AWS General Reference - AWS General Reference

setup.why: Customer engagements start with access questions, and a scoping document must state who holds which credentials. Knowing the credential types lets you write that section accurately.

setup.do: Create a local Git repository with a Markdown design doc skeleton, a decisions folder and a diagrams folder, and add a review section with one heading per pillar of the framework.
setup.done_when: The repository holds a design doc file with empty sections for scope, requirements, decisions, architecture, cost and one review heading per pillar.

source.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework - AWS Well-Architected Framework

setup.why: Every later step writes into this repository, so the design doc, the decision records and the diagrams stay versioned together. The pillar headings come from the framework introduction.

steps.do: Write a one-page scoping brief for a sample engagement, such as a document question answering assistant for a customer support team, listing what is in scope, what is out of scope, assumptions and the two trade-offs you expect to argue about.
steps.done_when: The scope section of the design doc lists in-scope items, out-of-scope items, assumptions and two named trade-offs.

source.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework - AWS Well-Architected Framework

steps.why: Scoping turns a vague request into a bounded commitment, and the framework introduction gives you the vocabulary of trade-offs between pillars. Naming the trade-offs up front tells the customer where decisions will be needed.

steps.do: Write the requirements section of the design doc by answering each compute criterion in the decision guide for your sample workload.
steps.done_when: The requirements section has one answered line per criterion in the guide, with unknowns marked as open questions.

source.title: Choosing an AWS compute service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: A useful design doc states requirements before solutions. The guide's criteria are a ready checklist of questions to put to a customer.

steps.do: Compare the compute options in the guide against your answers and write the options-considered section of the design doc with one chosen option and two rejected ones.
steps.done_when: The design doc names one chosen compute option and two rejected options, each with a one-line reason tied to a requirement.

source.title: Choosing an AWS compute service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Reviewers trust a design doc that shows the alternatives and why they lost. The comparison table gives you the facts to do that.

steps.do: Write your first architecture decision record for the compute choice, with status, context, decision and consequences, using the serverless section as evidence for the context.
steps.done_when: The decisions folder holds a numbered record whose consequences section lists at least one cost you accept.

source.title: Choosing an AWS compute service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: A decision record captures one decision in a form that outlives the engagement. The guide supplies the facts; the record format is your own short Markdown file in the decisions folder.

steps.do: Write a second decision record for which generative AI service the assistant uses, drawn from the choose table in the generative AI guide.
steps.done_when: A second numbered record exists and names the chosen service, the alternatives considered and the condition that would make you revisit it.

source.title: Choosing a generative AI service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: For this role the model service is usually the most contested decision. Writing it down with its alternatives stops it being reopened in every meeting.

steps.do: Write a third decision record for the data store, then mark it as superseded by a fourth record after you change one requirement, such as adding a need for semantic search.
steps.done_when: The third record shows status superseded and links to the fourth, which shows status accepted.

source.title: Choosing an AWS database service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Decision records are never edited after acceptance; they are superseded. Practising that once shows how a decision history stays honest.

steps.do: Create a C4 system context diagram and a container diagram in Mermaid in the diagrams folder, with the customer's users and existing systems outside the boundary and your chosen services as containers.
steps.done_when: Two diagrams render in your Markdown preview, and every container in the second maps to a service named in a decision record.

source.title: Choosing an AWS application integration service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: The context level is for customer stakeholders and the container level is for engineers. The integration guide helps you identify which external systems and message flows must appear.

steps.do: Label every arrow between containers with the integration service or pattern you pick from the guide, and add a short key under the diagram.
steps.done_when: No arrow in the container diagram is unlabelled, and the key explains each integration choice in one line.

source.title: Choosing an AWS application integration service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Unlabelled arrows hide the hardest parts of a design. Choosing queue, event bus or workflow for each one forces the integration decisions into the open.

steps.do: Write the cost section of the design doc, stating how the customer will track and cap spend and which cost trade-off you made against performance or reliability.
steps.done_when: The cost section names a tracking approach, a budget owner and one explicit trade-off with its reasoning.

source.title: Choosing an AWS cost management strategy - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: A scoped commitment without a cost view is not bounded. The guide's criteria tell you what to ask about budgets, visibility and ownership.

steps.do: Run a pillar review of the finished design doc by writing, under each pillar heading, one strength, one risk and one follow-up action; the AWS Well-Architected Tool in the console can hold the same review at no charge if you have an account.
steps.done_when: Every pillar heading has a strength, a risk and an action, and at least one risk has led to a change in the design doc or a new decision record.

source.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework - AWS Well-Architected Framework

steps.why: Checking against the standard pillars catches gaps a single author misses. It also gives the customer a familiar frame for the review meeting.

steps.do: Create a reusable engagement template in the repository from the criteria you used, then reproduce the requirements and options sections for a second scenario where the customer already runs containers.
steps.done_when: A template folder exists, and a second design doc built from it reaches a different compute decision with its own record.

source.title: Choosing an AWS container service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: A forward deployed engineer repeats this process for every customer, so it must be repeatable. Rerunning it on a different workload proves the template works and is not tied to one design.

steps.do: Reproduce the full pack for a production-like variant in which part of the workload must stay in the customer's own data centre, updating the scope, the decision records, the C4 diagrams and the pillar review.
steps.done_when: The repository holds a complete second pack in which the on-premises constraint is visible in the scope, in at least one decision record, in the container diagram and in the pillar review.

source.title: Choosing an AWS container service - AWS Decision Guides

steps.why: Real engagements come with constraints such as data residency and existing hardware. Reworking the whole pack under one hard constraint is the closest laptop substitute for a production engagement.
